blocks.source: Vol III, Introduction, § Anatomy of a Repair Trajectory
blocks.md: Up to this point, the stochastic computer map, the H·S·A exposure space, invariant closure, and horizon arithmetic have appeared one instrument at a time. During an actual run of the race-condition repair (a later section), all four act on the same sequence of steps at once. Every proposed edit tests the workspace boundary, draws down the turn and dollar budget, and produces compiler or test output that shapes the next decision.

blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Every turn passes context assembly, model invocation, validate-and-authorize, tool execution, observation, and assessment against the contract, and only the second phase belongs to the model.

questions.q: The section **Anatomy of a Repair Trajectory** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Every trajectory ends accepted, failed, unresolved, or escalated, budget exhaustion is unresolved rather than failure, and silent termination is a defect.
Every turn passes context assembly, model invocation, validate-and-authorize, tool execution, observation, and assessment against the contract, and only the second phase belongs to the model.
A model-directed loop is justified only where open-ended evidence must be interpreted and it raises acceptance by more than it inflates attempt cost under the same contract and verifier.

A system is agentic when a runtime, not a human, closes the proposal-action-observation loop, so the model's output is a proposal with no standing authority and enforcement, isolation, persistence, and completion checks belong to the runtime.
